items.stem: Which term is defined as "a reduction division in which a diploid nucleus divides twice to produce four genetically different haploid nuclei"?
items.answer: Meiosis
items.markingKey: Meiosis: a reduction division in which a diploid nucleus divides twice to produce four genetically different haploid nuclei.

items.stem: Explain why meiosis is necessary in sexually reproducing organisms.
items.answer: Gametes must be haploid so that when they fuse at fertilisation the diploid chromosome number is restored and stays constant from generation to generation; meiosis also produces variation.
items.markingKey: haploid gametes [1]; diploid restored at fertilisation [1]; variation [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how independent assortment produces genetic variation.
items.answer: In metaphase I each homologous pair lines up randomly on the equator, so the maternal or paternal chromosome may go to either pole; the number of combinations is 2ⁿ (n = haploid number).
items.markingKey: random orientation of pairs [1]; each gamete gets mixture [1]; 2ⁿ combinations [1] [3]

items.stem: Nadia is studying meiosis in a fruit fly, which has a diploid number of 8. Calculate the number of possible combinations of chromosomes in the gametes due to independent assortment alone.

Tomás is studying meiosis in a mosquito, which has a diploid number of 6. (a) State the number of chromosomes in a gamete. (b) Explain why the actual number of genetically different gametes is much greater than this.
items.answer: (a) 3 (b) Crossing over during prophase I produces new combinations of alleles within chromosomes.
items.markingKey: (a) n = 3 [1] (b) crossing over [1]; new combinations of alleles on chromatids [1] [2]

items.stem: Felix is studying meiosis in a human, which has a diploid number of 46. (a) Calculate the number of possible combinations of chromosomes in the gametes due to independent assortment alone. (b) A diploid cell of this organism in G1 contains 7 arbitrary units of DNA. State the DNA content of a cell at the end of meiosis I and of each gamete.
items.answer: (a) 8,388,608 (b) end of meiosis I: 7 units per cell; gamete: 3.5 units
items.markingKey: (a) 2ⁿ [1] = 2^23 = 8,388,608 [1] [2] (b) doubled to 14 after S phase, halved at meiosis I = 7 [1]; gamete 3.5 [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Istanbul draws diagrams of meiosis in a cell with 2n = 6, in which one homologous pair carries alleles A and a, and another carries B and b. (a) Explain why gametes produced by meiosis are genetically different from each other while cells produced by mitosis are identical. (b) State the number of chromosomes in each cell at the end of meiosis II.
items.answer: (a) Mitosis: no pairing, no crossing over, chromatids separate so daughter cells receive identical copies; meiosis: crossing over and independent assortment of homologues, plus halving of chromosome number. (b) 3
items.markingKey: (a) mitosis identical copies [1]; crossing over [1]; independent assortment [1] [3] (b) 3 [1]

items.stem: A student in Istanbul draws diagrams of meiosis in a cell with 2n = 4, in which one homologous pair carries alleles A and a, and another carries B and b. (a) Draw or describe the possible arrangements of these chromosomes at metaphase I and the gametes produced, ignoring crossing over. (b) Explain how crossing over between the A/a locus and the centromere would change the gametes from one cell. (c) State the number of chromosomes in each cell at the end of meiosis II.
items.answer: (a) Two arrangements: AB/ab or Ab/aB on the same side; gametes AB, ab, Ab, aB in equal proportions. (b) Each meiosis would then produce four different gametes, rather than two types, because one chromatid of each homologue exchanges the allele. (c) 2
items.markingKey: (a) two arrangements [1]; four gamete types [1] [2] (b) non-sister chromatids exchange alleles [1]; four different gametes from one cell [1] [2] (c) 2 [1]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "a cell or nucleus with one set of chromosomes (n)"?
items.answer: Haploid
items.markingKey: Haploid: a cell or nucleus with one set of chromosomes (n).

items.stem: At which stage of meiosis do homologous chromosomes separate?
items.answer: Anaphase I
items.markingKey: Homologues separate in anaphase I; chromatids in anaphase II.

items.stem: Explain how crossing over increases genetic variation.
items.answer: Non-sister chromatids of homologues break and rejoin at chiasmata, exchanging sections; this produces chromatids with new combinations of alleles of linked genes.
items.markingKey: chiasmata / exchange between non-sister chromatids [1]; new allele combinations [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis I.
items.answer: Prophase I: chromosomes condense, homologues pair into bivalents, crossing over; metaphase I: bivalents on equator, random orientation; anaphase I: homologues pulled to opposite poles; telophase I: two haploid nuclei.
items.markingKey: prophase I [1]; metaphase I [1]; anaphase I [1]; telophase I [1] [4]

items.stem: A photomicrograph of an anther cell shows that bivalents line up on the equator of the spindle, with random orientation of each pair. Which stage of meiosis is shown?
items.answer: Metaphase I
items.markingKey: Metaphase I: bivalents line up on the equator of the spindle, with random orientation of each pair.

items.stem: A cell from an organism with 2n = 6 is seen in anaphase II. Describe what is happening in the cell at this stage, and state how many chromatids are present in the cell (or each of the two cells if after meiosis I).
items.answer: Centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles. Chromatids: 6 per cell, separating into 3 per daughter nucleus.
items.markingKey: description [2]; correct chromatid number [1] [3]

items.stem: A student in Madrid draws diagrams of meiosis in a cell with 2n = 6, in which one homologous pair carries alleles A and a, and another carries B and b. (a) Explain how crossing over between the A/a locus and the centromere would change the gametes from one cell. (b) Explain why gametes produced by meiosis are genetically different from each other while cells produced by mitosis are identical. (c) State the number of chromosomes in each cell at the end of meiosis II.
items.answer: (a) Each meiosis would then produce four different gametes, rather than two types, because one chromatid of each homologue exchanges the allele. (b) Mitosis: no pairing, no crossing over, chromatids separate so daughter cells receive identical copies; meiosis: crossing over and independent assortment of homologues, plus halving of chromosome number. (c) 3
items.markingKey: (a) non-sister chromatids exchange alleles [1]; four different gametes from one cell [1] [2] (b) mitosis identical copies [1]; crossing over [1]; independent assortment [1] [3] (c) 3 [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "homozygous"?
options: The first filial generation: the offspring of a cross between two pure-breeding parents.
The alleles possessed by an organism for a particular gene or genes.
Having two identical alleles of a gene.
The observable characteristics of an organism, resulting from its genotype and the environment.
items.answer: Having two identical alleles of a gene.
items.markingKey: Homozygous: having two identical alleles of a gene.

items.stem: Explain why a carrier of a sex-linked recessive condition is always female.
items.answer: Females have two X chromosomes so can be heterozygous (one dominant, one recessive allele) without showing the condition; males have one X so a recessive allele is always expressed.
items.markingKey: females two X / heterozygous [1]; males hemizygous so always express [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a test cross can be used to determine the genotype of a tall pea plant.
items.answer: Cross it with a dwarf (tt) plant; if all offspring are tall the plant is TT; if about half are dwarf the plant is Tt.
items.markingKey: cross with tt [1]; interpretation of results [1] [2]

items.stem: In humans, haemoglobin type is controlled by a gene with two alleles, Hbᴬ and Hbˢ (codominant). A sickle cell trait individual with genotype HbᴬHbˢ is crossed with a sickle cell anaemia individual with genotype HbˢHbˢ. Draw a genetic diagram to show the expected genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring, and state the phenotypic ratio.
items.answer: 1 sickle cell trait : 1 sickle cell anaemia
items.markingKey: parental genotypes HbᴬHbˢ × HbˢHbˢ [1]; gametes Hbᴬ, Hbˢ and Hbˢ [1]; offspring genotypes from Punnett square [1]; phenotypes with ratio 1 sickle cell trait : 1 sickle cell anaemia [1] [4]

items.stem: In tomato plants, stem colour is controlled by a gene with two alleles, A and a (A dominant). A purple stem individual with genotype AA is crossed with a purple stem individual with genotype Aa. Draw a genetic diagram to show the expected genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring, and state the phenotypic ratio.
items.answer: all purple stem
items.markingKey: parental genotypes AA × Aa [1]; gametes A and A, a [1]; offspring genotypes from Punnett square [1]; phenotypes with ratio all purple stem [1] [4]

items.stem: In cattle, coat colour is controlled by a gene with two alleles, Cᴿ and Cᵂ (codominant). A red individual with genotype CᴿCᴿ is crossed with a white individual with genotype CᵂCᵂ. Use a genetic diagram to show the expected phenotypes of the offspring, and calculate how many of 200 offspring would be expected to be roan.
items.answer: all roan; expected roan: 1 × 200 = 200
items.markingKey: parental genotypes CᴿCᴿ × CᵂCᵂ [1]; gametes Cᴿ and Cᵂ [1]; offspring genotypes from Punnett square [1]; phenotypes with ratio all roan [1]; 1 × 200 = 200 [1] [5]

items.stem: Explain, using genetic diagrams, the inheritance of ABO blood groups and of haemophilia.
items.answer: ABO: three alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ (codominant), Iᵒ (recessive); six genotypes, four phenotypes; e.g. IᴬIᵒ × IᴮIᵒ gives A, B, AB, O 1:1:1:1. Haemophilia: X-linked recessive, XᴴXʰ × XᴴY → daughters XᴴXᴴ, XᴴXʰ; sons XᴴY, XʰY; half of sons affected; males hemizygous; females rarely affected.
items.markingKey: ABO alleles and dominance [2]; correct ABO diagram [2]; X-linkage explained [1]; correct haemophilia diagram [2] [7]

items.stem: Human ABO blood groups are controlled by three alleles: Iᴬ and Iᴮ (codominant) and Iᵒ (recessive). Chloe has genotype IᴬIᵒ (blood group A) and Felix has genotype IᴬIᴬ (blood group A). (a) Use a genetic diagram to show the possible blood groups of their children and the probability of each. (b) Explain why the observed numbers of offspring in such a cross usually differ from the expected ratio.
items.answer: (a) all group A (b) Fertilisation is random, so the ratio is a probability; with small numbers chance deviations are large; some genotypes may have lower survival.
items.markingKey: (a) gametes Iᴬ, Iᵒ and Iᴬ [1]; offspring genotypes [1]; blood groups and probabilities (all group A) [1] [3] (b) random fertilisation / chance [1]; small sample [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring of a cross between two heterozygotes for a gene showing complete dominance?
items.markingKey: Aa × Aa → 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa.

items.stem: Why do females rarely show sex-linked recessive conditions such as haemophilia?
options: The allele is on the Y chromosome
The allele is dominant in females
They need to inherit two copies of the recessive allele, one on each X chromosome
items.answer: They need to inherit two copies of the recessive allele, one on each X chromosome
items.markingKey: Males have only one X.

items.stem: A woman who is a carrier of haemophilia has children with a man without haemophilia. What proportion of their daughters are expected to have haemophilia?
items.markingKey: Daughters receive the father's Xᴴ.

items.stem: In humans, cystic fibrosis is controlled by a gene with two alleles, F and f (F dominant). An unaffected (carrier) individual with genotype Ff is crossed with an unaffected individual with genotype FF. What is the expected ratio of phenotypes in the offspring?
items.answer: all one phenotype
items.markingKey: Gametes F, f × F, F; offspring all unaffected.

items.stem: Human ABO blood groups are controlled by three alleles: Iᴬ and Iᴮ (codominant) and Iᵒ (recessive). Leila has genotype IᵒIᵒ (blood group O) and Ana has genotype IᴬIᵒ (blood group A). Which blood group is NOT possible among their children?
items.answer: Group AB
items.markingKey: Gametes Iᵒ/Iᵒ × Iᴬ/Iᵒ; possible children: 1 group A : 1 group O.

items.stem: Human ABO blood groups are controlled by three alleles: Iᴬ and Iᴮ (codominant) and Iᵒ (recessive). Elena has genotype IᵒIᵒ (blood group O) and Daniel has genotype IᴬIᴮ (blood group AB). Use a genetic diagram to show the possible blood groups of their children and the probability of each.
items.answer: 1 group A : 1 group B
items.markingKey: gametes Iᵒ and Iᴬ, Iᴮ [1]; offspring genotypes [1]; blood groups and probabilities (1 group A : 1 group B) [1] [3]

items.stem: A student in Cairo draws diagrams of meiosis in a cell with 2n = 6, in which one homologous pair carries alleles A and a, and another carries B and b. (a) Draw or describe the possible arrangements of these chromosomes at metaphase I and the gametes produced, ignoring crossing over. (b) Suggest why errors in meiosis such as non-disjunction can lead to conditions such as Down syndrome.
items.answer: (a) Two arrangements: AB/ab or Ab/aB on the same side; gametes AB, ab, Ab, aB in equal proportions. (b) If homologues or chromatids fail to separate, a gamete may have an extra chromosome; fertilisation gives a zygote with three copies (trisomy 21).
items.markingKey: (a) two arrangements [1]; four gamete types [1] [2] (b) non-disjunction [1]; extra chromosome / trisomy [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term is defined as "an offspring with a combination of alleles not found in either parent, produced by crossing over between linked genes"?
items.answer: Recombinant
items.markingKey: Recombinant: an offspring with a combination of alleles not found in either parent, produced by crossing over between linked genes.

items.stem: Explain how autosomal linkage changes the results of a dihybrid test cross.
items.answer: Linked alleles are on the same chromosome and pass to gametes together, so parental combinations are more frequent than expected (not 1 : 1 : 1 : 1); recombinants appear only if crossing over occurs between the loci, so they are fewer.
items.markingKey: alleles inherited together [1]; parental types more frequent [1]; recombinants from crossing over [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a 9 : 3 : 4 ratio is seen in the inheritance of coat colour in mice.
items.answer: One gene (A/a) determines whether pigment is made; homozygous aa animals are albino whatever the alleles of the second gene (B/b, black or brown); the aa class combines 3 + 1 of the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, giving 9 : 3 : 4.
items.markingKey: epistatic gene masks second gene [1]; aa all albino [1]; combines classes to 9 : 3 : 4 [1] [3]

items.stem: Ravi carried out a cross between double heterozygous sweet pea plants (complementary genes) and expected a 9 : 7 ratio. The observed numbers of offspring were class 1: 116, class 2: 84 (total 200). (a) Calculate the expected numbers for each class. (b) State the number of degrees of freedom for this test and explain how it is found.
items.answer: (a) 112.5, 87.5 (b) 1: the number of classes (2) minus one.
items.markingKey: (a) N × fraction: 112.5, 87.5 [1] (b) 1: the number of classes (2) minus one [1]

items.stem: Jonas carried out a cross between double heterozygous squash plants (dominant epistasis) and expected a 12 : 3 : 1 ratio. The observed numbers of offspring were class 1: 184, class 2: 40, class 3: 16 (total 240). (a) Calculate the expected numbers for each class. (b) State the number of degrees of freedom for this test and explain how it is found.
items.answer: (a) 180, 45, 15 (b) 2: the number of classes (3) minus one.
items.markingKey: (a) N × fraction: 180, 45, 15 [1] (b) 2: the number of classes (3) minus one [1]

items.stem: In squash plants, fruit colour is controlled by two unlinked genes: W (white, blocks colour) / w (allows colour), and Y (yellow) / y (green). Two double heterozygotes were crossed and produced 367 white, 81 yellow, 32 green offspring. (a) Explain the ratio of phenotypes obtained. (b) Explain what is meant by epistasis.
items.answer: (a) Close to 12 : 3 : 1: dominant epistasis: any W gives white fruit regardless of Y/y. (b) An interaction between two genes in which one gene affects or masks the expression of another.
items.markingKey: (a) expected ratio 12 : 3 : 1 [1]; epistatic interaction explained [2] [3] (b) An interaction between two genes in which one gene affects or masks the expression of another [1]

items.stem: In a test cross of a double heterozygote, 45% of offspring are each of two parental types and 5% each of two recombinant types. What is the recombination frequency?
Explain why 9 : 7 ratios are found in some dihybrid crosses, such as flower colour in sweet peas.
items.answer: Two genes control two steps in a pathway to the pigment; a dominant allele of both is needed for colour; any aa or bb genotype blocks the pathway, so 9 coloured : 7 white.
items.markingKey: two enzymes in pathway [1]; need dominant allele of both [1]; 9 : 7 [1] [3]

items.stem: In Drosophila, the genes for body and wings are on the same chromosome. A double heterozygote (EV/ev) was test-crossed with a homozygous recessive. Offspring: grey body, normal wings 400; ebony body, vestigial wings 400; grey body, vestigial wings 100; ebony body, normal wings 100. Calculate the recombination frequency.

In squash plants, fruit colour is controlled by two unlinked genes: W (white, blocks colour) / w (allows colour), and Y (yellow) / y (green). Two double heterozygotes were crossed and produced 366 white, 87 yellow, 27 green offspring. (a) Explain the ratio of phenotypes obtained. (b) Draw a genetic diagram to show the gametes and the genotypes that give each phenotype.
items.answer: (a) Close to 12 : 3 : 1: dominant epistasis: any W gives white fruit regardless of Y/y. (b) Gametes WY, Wy, wY, wy from each parent; 16 combinations grouped into white, yellow, green.
items.markingKey: (a) expected ratio 12 : 3 : 1 [1]; epistatic interaction explained [2] [3] (b) four gamete types [1]; genotypes assigned to phenotypes [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "operator"?
options: A protein that binds to DNA (e.g. at a promoter) and switches transcription of a gene on or off.
The region of DNA to which RNA polymerase binds to begin transcription.
The region of DNA next to the structural genes to which a repressor protein binds.
An enzyme that is synthesised only when its substrate is present, such as β-galactosidase.
items.answer: The region of DNA next to the structural genes to which a repressor protein binds.
items.markingKey: Operator: the region of DNA next to the structural genes to which a repressor protein binds.

items.stem: Explain how the lac operon allows E. coli to produce β-galactosidase only when lactose is present.
items.answer: Regulatory gene makes repressor that binds operator, blocking RNA polymerase; lactose binds repressor, changing its shape so it leaves the operator; RNA polymerase binds promoter and transcribes lacZ, lacY, lacA; enzymes made; saves energy when lactose absent.
items.markingKey: repressor binds operator [1]; lactose binds repressor / shape change [1]; RNA polymerase transcribes [1]; saves resources [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain how transcription factors control gene expression in eukaryotes.
items.answer: Transcription factors bind to specific DNA sequences such as promoters; some help RNA polymerase bind and start transcription, others prevent it; different cells contain different factors so different genes are expressed.
items.markingKey: bind specific DNA [1]; activate or repress RNA polymerase binding [1]; cell-specific expression [1] [3]

items.stem: Ethan studies a strain of E. coli in which a mutation in the regulatory gene produces a repressor that cannot bind to the operator. Predict and explain the effect on the production of β-galactosidase.
items.answer: Β-galactosidase is made all the time (constitutively), with or without lactose.
items.markingKey: prediction [1]; explanation in terms of repressor / operator / RNA polymerase [2] [3]

items.stem: Explain the effect on the lac operon if a mutation in the regulatory gene produces a repressor that cannot bind to the operator.
items.answer: Β-galactosidase is made all the time (constitutively), with or without lactose.
items.markingKey: prediction [1]; explanation in terms of repressor / operator / RNA polymerase [2] [3]

items.stem: E. coli were grown in a medium containing glucose only; at 20 minutes lactose was added. β-galactosidase activity was negligible before 20 minutes and rose rapidly from about 23 minutes. (a) Explain why β-galactosidase activity was negligible before lactose was added. (b) Explain the advantage to E. coli of this control mechanism.
items.answer: (a) The repressor protein made by the regulatory gene was bound to the operator, so RNA polymerase could not transcribe lacZ. (b) Enzymes are made only when needed, so energy and amino acids are not wasted making unnecessary proteins.
items.markingKey: (a) repressor on operator [1]; no transcription [1] [2] (b) Enzymes are made only when needed [1]; so energy and amino acids are not wasted making unnecessary proteins [1] [2]

items.stem: An E. coli strain makes β-galactosidase even when no lactose is present. Which mutation could cause this?
options: A mutation in the promoter so RNA polymerase cannot bind
A mutation in the operator so the repressor cannot bind
A mutation so the repressor binds lactose more tightly
items.answer: A mutation in the operator so the repressor cannot bind
items.markingKey: Constitutive expression.

items.stem: Explain the role of DELLA proteins in the response of a seed to gibberellin.
items.answer: DELLA proteins bind to transcription factors (PIF) and prevent transcription of genes such as amylase; gibberellin binds a receptor and causes DELLA to be destroyed (ubiquitination/proteasome), so PIF can promote transcription.
items.markingKey: DELLA inhibit transcription factor [1]; gibberellin causes DELLA breakdown [1]; genes transcribed [1] [3]

items.stem: Freya studies a strain of E. coli in which a mutation in the promoter prevents RNA polymerase from binding. Predict and explain the effect on the production of β-galactosidase.
items.answer: None of the three enzymes is made, even with lactose present.
items.markingKey: prediction [1]; explanation in terms of repressor / operator / RNA polymerase [2] [3]

items.stem: E. coli were grown in a medium containing glucose only; at 40 minutes lactose was added. β-galactosidase activity was negligible before 40 minutes and rose rapidly from about 43 minutes. (a) Explain why β-galactosidase activity was negligible before lactose was added. (b) Explain the advantage to E. coli of this control mechanism. (c) Compare gene control in the lac operon with control by transcription factors in eukaryotes.
items.answer: (a) The repressor protein made by the regulatory gene was bound to the operator, so RNA polymerase could not transcribe lacZ. (b) Enzymes are made only when needed, so energy and amino acids are not wasted making unnecessary proteins. (c) Lac: repressor binds operator next to genes transcribed together on one mRNA. Eukaryotes: transcription factors bind promoter/enhancer of individual genes; can activate or repress; each gene usually has its own promoter.
items.markingKey: (a) repressor on operator [1]; no transcription [1] [2] (b) Enzymes are made only when needed [1]; so energy and amino acids are not wasted making unnecessary proteins [1] [2] (c) operon vs individual genes [1]; repressor vs activating/repressing factors [1] [2]

items.stem: During which stage does crossing over occur?
items.answer: Prophase I
items.markingKey: Chiasmata form between non-sister chromatids in prophase I.

items.stem: A cell has 12 chromosomes in G1 of the cell cycle. How many chromosomes are in each cell at the end of meiosis II?
items.markingKey: Haploid number.

items.stem: A student in Hanoi states: "Meiosis produces two diploid cells." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Meiosis produces four haploid cells (in animals usually gametes).

items.answer: A and B only

items.stem: Explain the inheritance of tortoiseshell coat colour in cats, which is almost always found in females.
items.answer: Coat colour gene on X with codominant alleles Xᴼ (orange) and Xᴮ (black); females XᴼXᴮ show both colours (tortoiseshell); males have one X so are either orange or black.
items.markingKey: X-linked [1]; codominance in heterozygous females [1]; males have one allele [1] [3]

items.stem: Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele h of a gene on the X chromosome (dominant allele H). A woman with genotype XʰXʰ (haemophilia) has children with a man with genotype XᴴY (blood clots normally), in a family referred to a genetic clinic in Toronto. What is the probability that a son of this couple has haemophilia?
items.markingKey: daughter carrier (blood clots normally): 1/2; son haemophilia: 1/2 of all children. Probability that a son is affected = 1.

items.stem: In pea plants, round (R) is dominant to wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) is dominant to green (y). The genes are on different chromosomes. Pea plants with genotype RrYy are crossed with pea plants with genotype Rryy. What is the expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring?
items.markingKey: Gametes RY, Ry, rY, ry × Ry, ry; 3 round, yellow : 3 round, green : 1 wrinkled, yellow : 1 wrinkled, green.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "epistasis"?
options: An offspring with a combination of alleles not found in either parent, produced by crossing over between linked genes.
A statistical test used to find whether the difference between observed and expected frequencies of categorical data is significant.
The percentage of offspring that are recombinants; it increases with the distance between linked genes.
The interaction of two genes in which one gene affects or masks the expression of another.
items.answer: The interaction of two genes in which one gene affects or masks the expression of another.

items.stem: Explain why the chi-squared test is used rather than simply comparing numbers.
items.answer: Observed results always vary from expected by chance; the test gives a probability that the difference is due to chance, so we can decide objectively whether it is significant.

items.stem: Explain how autosomal linkage and epistasis can each cause the results of a dihybrid cross to differ from a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio, and how the chi-squared test is used to evaluate such results.
items.answer: Linkage: genes on same chromosome, alleles inherited together, parental types in excess, recombinants via crossing over, RF. items.stem: A student in Lisbon draws diagrams of meiosis in a cell with 2n = 6, in which one homologous pair carries alleles A and a, and another carries B and b. (a) Draw or describe the possible arrangements of these chromosomes at metaphase I and the gametes produced, ignoring crossing over. (b) Explain why gametes produced by meiosis are genetically different from each other while cells produced by mitosis are identical. (c) Suggest why errors in meiosis such as non-disjunction can lead to conditions such as Down syndrome.
items.answer: (a) Two arrangements: AB/ab or Ab/aB on the same side; gametes AB, ab, Ab, aB in equal proportions. (b) Mitosis: no pairing, no crossing over, chromatids separate so daughter cells receive identical copies; meiosis: crossing over and independent assortment of homologues, plus halving of chromosome number. (c) If homologues or chromatids fail to separate, a gamete may have an extra chromosome; fertilisation gives a zygote with three copies (trisomy 21).

items.stem: E. coli were grown in a medium containing glucose only; at 40 minutes lactose was added. β-galactosidase activity was negligible before 40 minutes and rose rapidly from about 43 minutes. (a) Explain why β-galactosidase activity was negligible before lactose was added. (b) Explain why β-galactosidase activity rose after lactose was added. (c) Explain the advantage to E. coli of this control mechanism.
items.answer: (a) The repressor protein made by the regulatory gene was bound to the operator, so RNA polymerase could not transcribe lacZ. (b) Lactose entered (via a few permease molecules), bound to the repressor, changed its shape; repressor left the operator; RNA polymerase transcribed lacZ, lacY, lacA; mRNA translated. (c) Enzymes are made only when needed, so energy and amino acids are not wasted making unnecessary proteins.
items.markingKey: (a) repressor on operator [1]; no transcription [1] [2] (b) lactose binds repressor [1]; repressor released [1]; transcription and translation [1] [3] (c) Enzymes are made only when needed [1]; so energy and amino acids are not wasted making unnecessary proteins [1] [2]
